title: Cap. VIII: Augustine rejects foresight of Esau's evil and Jacob's good alike as causes
pass_a_gloss: To this also is added that Augustine (than whom no one treated this cause more learnedly or more holily) as much denies that the foresighted evil works of Esau were the cause that he was reprobated by God, as he denies that the foresighted good works of Jacob were the cause that he was elected by God. See the Enchiridion to Laurentius chapter 98, To Simplicianus book 1 question 2, and Epistle 105, where he equally rejects the sentence of those who say that God hated this one or loved that one of those not yet born, because he foresaw their future works. And Epistle 106 openly teaches that God by loving discerns those whom no merits discern. As therefore he does not admit foresight of good merits to have been the cause of election, so neither does he grant foresight of evils to have been the reason of reprobation. For where on one side good acts are considered, for example of believing, of obeying, of persevering, on the other evil acts opposite to these, it is clear that those are considered as discerned by merits. But let us come unto the sentence of Corvinus.
pass_b_english: Add Augustine — no one treated this cause more learnedly or holily: he denies as much that Esau's foresighted evil works were the cause of his reprobation as that Jacob's foresighted good works were the cause of his election. See Enchiridion to Laurentius 98, To Simplicianus 1.2, and Epistle 105, where he equally rejects those who say God hated or loved the not-yet-born because he foresaw their future works. Epistle 106 openly teaches that God by loving discerns those whom no merits discern. As he will not admit foresight of good merits as election's cause, so he will not grant foresight of evils as reprobation's reason. For where good acts — believing, obeying, persevering — stand on one side and opposite evil acts on the other, those are clearly regarded as discerned by merits. But let us come to Corvinus's sentence.
source_text: Huc etiam accedit quod Augustinus (quo nemo doctius aut sanctius hanc causam tractavit) tam negat praevisa mala opera Esavi fuisse causam quod a Deo reprobaretur, quam praevisa bona opera Jacobi negat causam fuisse quod is a Deo eligeretur. Videte Enchir. ad Laurent. cap. 98, Ad Simpl. lib. 1. quaest. 2, et Epist. 105, ubi illorum sententiam qui inquiunt Deum nondum natorum vel hunc odisse vel illum dilexisse, quia eorum futura opera praevidebat, ex aequo rejicit. Et Epist. 106 aperte docet, Deum diligendo eos discernere, quos merita nulla discernunt. Sicut igitur praevisionem bonorum meritorum non admittit causam fuisse electionis, ita nec praevisionem malorum concedit fuisse rationem reprobationis. Nam ubi ex una parte considerantur boni actus, puta credendi, obediendi, perseverandi, ex altera mali actus hisce oppositi, illos ut meritis discretos considerari perspicuum est. Sed ad Corvini sententiam veniamus.
